study.title: 1 Chronicles 21 The census, the judgment, and the altar that holds the plague
study.overview: This chapter shows how a census motivated by pride and distrust brought judgment on Israel, but also how David's repentance paved the way for God's mercy. The text is not just about counting men; it reveals the tension between sin, discipline, intercession, and restoration. The culmination is the construction of an altar in the threshing floor of Ornã, a place that becomes decisive for the future worship of Israel.

outline.title: David orders the census, despite the warning of Joab
outline.explanation: Satan urges David to tell the people. Joab realizes that the initiative can bring damage to Israel, but the commandment of the king prevails. The survey is done, but already with signs of resistance and incompleteness, because Levi and Benjamin do not enter the count.

outline.title: God displeases, David repents and receives a choice of judgment
outline.explanation: David's act displeasure to the Lord, and the immediate answer is discipline over Israel. David confesses his sin and asks forgiveness, but the Lord, through Gad, presents three ways of affliction. David prefers to fall into the hands of God, relying on the abundance of divine mercy.

outline.title: The plague, the vision of the angel, and the intercession of David
outline.explanation: The plague kills many in Israel, and the angel of the Lord advances against Jerusalem until it is restrained. David sees the angel with the sword and acknowledges his guilt, asking that the punishment fall upon him and his house. Then the Lord commandes David to raise an altar in the middle of the Rim of Ornaman Jebusite.

outline.title: The purchase of the threw, the sacrifice and the suspension of destruction
outline.explanation: David obeys, buys the place for a fair price and refuses to offer God something that costs him nothing. He raises up the altar, offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and God responds with fire from heaven. The plague ceases, but David cannot go to the tabernacle at Gibeon, because the fear before the angel's sword prevents him from consulting God there.

study.context: The chapter connects to an episode already narrated in Samuel, but here the focus is different: the chronicler highlights the political scandal and more the path leading to the altar and the preparation of the future temple. The text also mentions that the tabernacle of Moses was still in Gibeon, while the recent altar was in the threshing floor of Ornan. This helps to show a transition in the mode of worship and in the place where God receives the offerings linked to the deliverance of Jerusalem.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that national sin is not trivial before God, even when action seems administrative or strategic. The count of the people themselves is not presented as neutral; the problem is in the heart of David, especially in pride and undue confidence in military force. The text also shows that God uses agents and circumstances to execute his purpose, while not failing to hold the sinner accountable. At the same time, divine discipline does not eliminate mercy: David runs to the grace of the Lord, and God himself interrupts judgment when the altar is lifted and the sacrifice is offered. The chapter also anticipates the centrality of the place of worship, for the purchased threshing floor becomes a point of convergence between repentance, atonement and future cult of the people.

scholarViews.insight: The chronicler interprets the action of Satan as real opposition against God and humanity, but also as something that, without realizing, ends up serving divine purposes.
The main root of David's sin in the counting of the people is the pride of the heart, and this ambition brings great offense before God.
David builds the altar on the threshing-fight of Ornã, and before the fear provoked by the angel's sword, he does not go to Gibeon to inquire of God.

questions: What does the text reveal about the difference between a seemingly technical decision and a decision born of pride?
Why did David prefer to fall into the hands of the Lord, and what does this teach about confidence in the mercy of God?
How do the purchase of the threws and the altar show that worship and repentance require a concrete answer?
study.practice: Examine whether your decisions are moved by faith or by need for control. Quickly confess any pride that you want to measure your security by numbers, results or power. When there is discipline of God, do not run away from it; run to him. And learn from David to offer to God what has real cost: time, obedience, generosity, and sincere repentance.
study.uncertainty: The chapter mentions the angel of the Lord and the fire of heaven, but does not detail mechanically how these signs occurred. Nor does it explain in depth why the census was specifically so offensive beyond the perception of divine displeasure and indications of pride and undue dependence on military force. The notes provided suggest connections to the parallel chapter in Samuel, but this synthesis avoided using information not present in the base text and notes.
